title: Symbol and Archetype
excerpt: Medusa as what happens when you don't take control of the great conflict. Athena as what happens when you do.

sections.title: Athena
sections.kicker: "i made up the following and do not know greek mythology butttt this is what i want to see."
body: The shield shows a picture of one of the greatest conflicts in greek mythology between the Gods and giants (the giants are the people i think aka mortals aka us). in the middle of shield that has the depiction shows medusas head in the dead center. Other things to note are Athena (the Goddess of wisdom) is shown to be holding the shield as if she has tamed 'the great conflict'. Adjacent to the shield sits a great snake, who is tamed and seems to obey the Goddess of wisdom. on the right hand Athena is holding nike who represents victory or 'that which comes from taming the chaos'. As the story goes, Athena helped perseus slay medusa. As a gift perseus gave the head to athena, and it is shown on her chest.

I like to see this as the following: Medusa, the greatest figure for chaos, she herself represents what happens when you do not take control of the great conflict. what happens is the chaos consumes you and you become like her in the fact that your ears are surrounded by decieving snakes growing in your head. you are consumed by the chaos until you are left with nothing and become frozen like stone.

however, when you embrace certain feminine archetypes or 'right brained' thinking, and balance both your hemispheres (the state of the union). you begin to embody athena by becoming the archetype of feminine wisdom itself. only in this wisdom can you slay the head of medusa by not staring into her eyes which decieve you first, through your wisdom. here you can slay her head, and now you have tamed the serpents and the chaos is bent to your will and your order, hence the snake standing firmly and obediently beside her. So the great conflict is under athenas power, and she has now achieved victory over herself and everything, hence nike.
